refs.quote: The water was the humidum radicale (radical moisture), which stood for the anima media natura or anima mundi imprisoned in matter
refs.note: Carrier: the alchemists from Democritus and Komarios onward, whose conception of the miraculous water Jung is reporting here; not his own psychological decoding.

qualifiers.scope: the decapitation in section III, v bis of the vision
qualifiers.condition: when it is struck off
qualifiers.modality: “therefore” — Jung’s inference from the meaning of the head in alchemy
qualifiers.note: The text’s grammatical subject is the decapitation, not the head; the condition carries that, so the recomposed claim states the same thing. Ground: for Zosimos and the later alchemists the head meant the “omega element” or “round element,” a synonym for the arcane substance.

refs.quote: The decapitation in section III, v bis therefore signifies the obtaining of the arcane substance.
Just as the angel Amnael brings the arcane substance with him, so the “Meridian of the Sun” is himself a representation of it.
the initiate named the “Meridian of the Sun” himself represents the arcane substance.
refs.note: Hedged in this paragraph: 'we shall hardly go wrong in supposing that'.

refs.quote: an indication of the psychic nature of the arcanum, for the head of a man signifies above all the seat of consciousness.
refs.correction_note: stage2: "an indication of" is asserted content, not a hedge — confidence medium->high (reverse-direction hedge fix)
refs.note: Hedged: Jung claims only 'an indication'.

qualifiers.carrier: the sacrificer, who belongs to the same equation
qualifiers.modality: an inference: “it follows that”
qualifiers.note: The text says the three “are three different aspects of the same principle,” not that they are numerically identical.

refs.quote: it follows that Ion, the uroboros, and the sacrificer are essentially the same.

qualifiers.scope: “the reduction to order, through reflection, of apparently chaotic fragments of the unconscious which have broken through into consciousness”
qualifiers.modality: a psychological parallel drawn by Jung, not an identity
qualifiers.note: Subject node dismemberment = the dismembering of the victim in the vision of Zosimos.

refs.quote: The psychological parallel to this is the reduction to order, through reflection, of apparently chaotic fragments of the unconscious

qualifiers.scope: the temple “built of a ‘single stone’”
qualifiers.modality: “obvious” — Jung’s reading of the symbolism

refs.quote: The temple built of a “single stone” is an obvious paraphrase of the lapis.

qualifiers.scope: the making of the vessel “by a kind of squaring of the circle” — “essentially a psychic operation, the creation of an inner readiness to accept the archetype of the self in whatever subjective form it appears”
qualifiers.modality: Jung’s psychological reading of Dorn’s view of the vessel
qualifiers.note: The text’s subject is the making of the vessel; the scope carries that, so the frozen subject does not change the claim.

refs.quote: It is essentially a psychic operation, the creation of an inner readiness to accept the archetype of the self
refs.note: Anaphora resolved in the cited paragraph: 'It' = the vessel, which Dorn says must be made 'by a kind of squaring of the circle'.

qualifiers.scope: the temple of the vision, as the site inside which the transformation process runs
qualifiers.modality: Jung's gloss on the vision, given as what “is perceived” when consciousness dawns
qualifiers.note: “that is, in the head” is an identification of the temple with the head, so the only predicate the frozen subject and object support is the copula; the second proposition packed into the original relation (that the transformation process runs inside the temple) is carried as a split.

refs.quote: the transformation process is taking place inside the temple, that is, in the head.

qualifiers.scope: in civilized man
qualifiers.note: the object node is singular; the text says “projections.”

refs.quote: Consciousness develops in civilized man by the acquisition of knowledge and by the withdrawal of projections.
The lapis signifies the inner man, the ἄνθρωπος πνενματικός , the natura abscondita which the alchemists sought to set free.
It symbolizes man, or rather, the inner man, and the paradoxical statements about it are really descriptions and definitions of this inner man.

qualifiers.carrier: the body, the other term the anima links
qualifiers.note: the text's phrase is “the link between body and spirit”; the body is held in carrier rather than embedded in the predicate, so the verb stays a clean phrase. The immediate subject of the sentence is Pandora/Eve, who “played the part” of the anima; the predicate quoted is a general statement about the anima.

refs.quote: She played the part, therefore, of the anima, who functions as the link between body and spirit

qualifiers.scope: in Khunrath's sixteenth-century formulation of the “theological” position of the lapis
qualifiers.modality: reported by Jung as Khunrath's formulation, not asserted in Jung's own voice
qualifiers.note: the equation is the one Khunrath made; attributing it in the verb would credit Jung with it, so the attribution sits in scope and modality.

refs.quote: In the sixteenth century Khunrath formulated for the first time the “theological” position of the lapis: it was the filius macrocosmi
refs.note: Carrier: Khunrath, who first formulated the 'theological' position of the lapis in the sixteenth century.

qualifiers.scope: the stone as the “midmost” of Ostanes' saying, which draws near to the highest and is made one with it
qualifiers.note: the text's full predicate is “the mediator which unites the opposites”; “mediator” is a role name for the same act of uniting, not a second claim, so it is recorded here rather than split off.

refs.quote: This “midmost” is the stone, the mediator which unites the opposites.
refs.note: Subject resolved in the cited paragraph: the 'midmost' of the Ostanes saying is the stone.

qualifiers.carrier: the idea of a transcendent totality, which coincides with what analytical psychology calls the self
qualifiers.note: the text's identity runs between the transcendent totality the lapis represents and the self; the mediating term is held in carrier so the predicate can stay “represents” rather than absorbing the coincidence.

refs.quote: the lapis represents the idea of a transcendent totality which coincides with what analytical psychology calls the self.

qualifiers.carrier: the divine water, for which the uroboros stands as symbol and of which the same is predicated
qualifiers.note: the object of “means” in the text is the deus absconditus; matter is only where he is hidden. Any clean verb between uroboros and matter would state a different claim, so the god is embedded in the predicate, as the third lesson allows, and flagged here.

refs.quote: the divine water or its symbol, the uroboros, means nothing other than the deus absconditus , the god hidden in matter

qualifiers.note: only the article is dropped from the extracted string; “or serpent” is an alias of the subject, not a further claim.

refs.quote: The dragon, or serpent, represents the initial state of unconsciousness
refs.correction_note: stage1: §118 asserts the INITIAL STATE of unconsciousness; attach converted to a stage-specific edge rather than inflating the general symbol equation

qualifiers.scope: the mystical side of alchemy, as distinct from its historical aspect
qualifiers.modality: “to all appearances”
qualifiers.note: the text specifies the manner — a concretization “in projected and symbolic form” — and its object as “the process of individuation.”

refs.quote: To all appearances, it is a concretization, in projected and symbolic form, of the process of individuation.

qualifiers.carrier: the thought “God under me,” which the text says is implicit in all alchemy and is the actual term the Christian standpoint cannot accommodate
qualifiers.note: the incompatibility the text states is with that thought rather than with alchemy as such, so the thought is held in carrier and its implicitness in alchemy is carried as a split. The sentence also predicates the same of “the truth of the Church,” a co-subject outside this edge's frozen subject, and frames the whole as what Paracelsus failed to see.

refs.quote: the truth of the Church and the Christian standpoint could never get along with the thought implicit in all alchemy, “God under me.”

qualifiers.scope: in alchemical tradition, long before Paracelsus and before Melchior Cibinensis' Mass
qualifiers.modality: reported by Jung as the received view (“had been regarded as”), not his own identification
qualifiers.note: the passive attributive verb of the text cannot be kept together with “allegory” inside the token budget; “counts as” preserves the reputational force while the attribution is carried in scope and modality. The text's subject is “the filius or lapis philosophorum.”

refs.quote: long before this the filius or lapis philosophorum had been regarded as an allegory of Christ
refs.note: the alchemical tradition (context: Melchior Cibinensis presenting the opus as a Mass), rendered by Jung

qualifiers.carrier: alchemy, whose aim the begetting is
qualifiers.modality: stated as the aim of alchemy, not as an accomplished fact
qualifiers.note: “in the shape of” is rendered “as”; “this light” in the quote is the light of nature of the preceding sentences.

refs.quote: so it is the aim of alchemy to beget this light in the shape of the filius philosophorum

qualifiers.carrier: human art, the extracting agent
qualifiers.scope: in the alchemical teaching Jung is expounding, set against Christ, in whom God himself became man
qualifiers.note: the second half of the original predicate is a distinct claim with its own object and is carried as a split; the means there (“by means of the opus”) survives only in the split's basis quote, since split claims have no qualifier slot.

refs.quote: the filius philosophorum was extracted from matter by human art and, by means of the opus, made into a new light-bringer
refs.correction_note: stage2: doctrinal content reported, asserts->reports
refs.note: alchemical teaching rendered in contrast with Christian doctrine — carrier: the alchemists

qualifiers.carrier: Paracelsus, who supplies the name Archeus for the inner heaven or homo maximus
qualifiers.modality: Jung's identification, hedged by him as “undoubtedly”
qualifiers.note: Paracelsus names the figure Archeus; the equation with the Primordial Man is Jung's. A predicate of the form “is Paracelsus's name for” would credit Paracelsus with that equation, so the naming stays in carrier and the equation is marked as Jung's in modality.

refs.quote: Elsewhere he is called Archeus ... Undoubtedly this is the Primordial Man

qualifiers.modality: hedged twice in the text: “seems to be a kind of”
qualifiers.note: the ground given is that there are as many Iliastri as there are men, each holding together one man's peculiar combination of qualities.

refs.quote: It therefore seems to be a kind of universal formative principle and principle of individuation.

qualifiers.carrier: his chemical work, which the mental operation accompanies simultaneously
qualifiers.scope: in the Paracelsist tradition, where imaginatio is the active power of the astrum or higher man within
qualifiers.note: “by means of the imagination” is compressed to “by”; the operation's stated purpose (to cleanse the impure admixture and bring about the “confirmation” of the mind) is not carried in the predicate.

refs.quote: the artifex accompanies his chemical work with a simultaneous mental operation which is performed by means of the imagination

qualifiers.scope: among all the Paracelsan concepts; the term compared is the modern concept of the unconscious
qualifiers.note: the grounds given are the Aquaster's watery, “psychic” nature, its “necrocomic” functioning and its role as birthplace of the spiritus vitae.

refs.quote: Of all the Paracelsan concepts, therefore, the Aquaster comes closest to the modern concept of the unconscious.

qualifiers.note: the text's claim is comparative — “a more specific principle of individuation than the Iliaster” — and the comparison with the Iliaster cannot ride in the predicate within the token budget, so it is recorded here. Ares is introduced as “an intuitive concept for a preconscious, creative, and formative principle.”

refs.quote: It is thus a more specific principle of individuation than the Iliaster

qualifiers.scope: for anyone familiar with the subliminal processes of psychic transformation
qualifiers.modality: “clearly”

refs.quote: For anyone familiar with the subliminal processes of psychic transformation, Melusina is clearly an anima figure.

qualifiers.modality: Jung's reading of what Michael Maier means (“In reality it is…”), against Maier's chemical sense of antimony
qualifiers.note: the superlatives of the text — “from the highest place into the darkest depths” — do not fit the predicate and are recorded here. The two other propositions in the original relation are carried as splits.

refs.quote: In reality it is the secret transformative substance, which fell from the highest place into the darkest depths of matter where it awaits deliverance.

qualifiers.scope: the sea in the alchemists' usage, their mare nostrum
qualifiers.note: the text's predicate nominal is “their own darkness, the unconscious”; “their own darkness” names the same predicate and is not a second claim.

refs.quote: The sea ( mare nostrum ) of the alchemists is their own darkness, the unconscious.

qualifiers.scope: as concepts: the psychic centre on one side, the self on the other
qualifiers.modality: “psychologically”
qualifiers.note: the centre meant is the psychic centre whose activation and development the retorta distillatio ex medio centri produces; that production is a separate claim and is carried as a split rather than as a condition, since the text does not make the coincidence conditional on the distillatio.

refs.quote: results in the activation and development of a psychic centre, a concept that coincides psychologically with that of the self

qualifiers.carrier: Ruland, in whose lexicon the definition stands
qualifiers.note: Ruland's definiens is “the regenerated spiritual man in us, the heavenly body implanted in us Christians by the Holy Ghost through the most Holy Sacraments”; “inner man” is the graph's term for it, and Jung goes on to deny that Paracelsus meant the inner man in the Christian sense. Bodenstein and Dorn's rival reading (“efficacity of things”) is not carried by this edge.

refs.quote: the regenerated spiritual man in us, the heavenly body implanted in us Christians by the Holy Ghost through the most Holy Sacraments

qualifiers.scope: hidden in the very darkness of nature, which without it would not be darkness
qualifiers.note: the cited quote names neither term; the identification rests on a later sentence of the same paragraph — “his whole creative yearning, belonged to the lumen naturae, the divine spark buried in the darkness.” “Scintilla” is the graph's Latin label for that spark, not Jung's word here.

refs.quote: They discover that in the very darkness of nature a light is hidden, a little spark without which the darkness would not be darkness.
refs.vocabulary_note: cross-vendor PARTIAL (b-cw13-3): §197 says 'little spark'/'divine spark'; scintilla is the graph's standing node, wording preserved in the relation — both-defensible

qualifiers.note: the text's term is “union of the natures,” stated contrastively against “separation of the natures”; the graph's object node generalizes it to union of opposites. The negated alternative is not carried as a separate claim.

refs.quote: Not separation of the natures but union of the natures was the goal of alchemy.
refs.vocabulary_note: cross-vendor PARTIAL (b-cw13-3): text says 'union of the natures'; the paragraph's own gloss ('Here the opposites unite') licenses union-of-opposites — both-defensible

qualifiers.carrier: the mortal man, who is the one approximated to him
qualifiers.modality: possibility, not accomplishment: “can be approximated”
qualifiers.note: the direction of the text's sentence is from mortal man to the Original Man by means of the opus; with the subject and object frozen as they are, the passive predicate keeps the same claim and the approaching party is held in carrier. The identification of the homo maximus with the deathless Original Man is a separate claim and is carried as a split.

refs.quote: that of the deathless Original Man, to whom the mortal man can be approximated by means of the alchemical opus
refs.correction_note: stage1: the identification carries "probably only" — confidence high->medium

qualifiers.carrier: the traditional quadripartite man, whose all-encompassing wholeness it is
qualifiers.modality: hedged: “it would not be overbold to conclude”
qualifiers.note: the correspondence with the quadripartite man is the other conjunct of the text's predicate and is carried as a split.

refs.quote: the four Scaiolae correspond to the traditional quadripartite man and express his all-encompassing wholeness

qualifiers.scope: as functions of consciousness, and particularly as imaginatio, speculatio, phantasia and fides
qualifiers.note: the text's full predicate is “stimulate Melusina, the water-nixie, to change herself into human form.” The purpose clause cannot stand after the frozen object, and asserting the change as accomplished would go beyond this paragraph, so it is recorded here. “Intervene” in the same sentence has no object and is not carried.

refs.quote: As functions of consciousness … they “intervene” and stimulate Melusina, the water-nixie, to change herself into human form.

qualifiers.carrier: the Wise Old Man, the second archetype flowing together with the anima
qualifiers.scope: in the symbolic phenomenology of Mercurius
qualifiers.note: the text's subject is the pair of archetypes; with only one of them as subject the predicate reads elliptically, and the other is held in carrier rather than embedded.

refs.quote: two empirically very common archetypes, namely the anima and the Wise Old Man … flow together in the symbolic phenomenology of Mercurius

qualifiers.carrier: his rigorous solitude together with his preoccupation with the endless obscurities of the work, which the text names as what was sufficient to activate the unconscious
qualifiers.modality: stated as sufficient cause (“was sufficient to activate”)
qualifiers.note: the grammatical subject in the text is the solitude, not the artifex; the artifex is the one whose solitude and preoccupation do the activating, so agency is moved to him and the actual agent held in carrier.

refs.quote: This rigorous solitude, together with his preoccupation with the endless obscurities of the work, was sufficient to activate the unconscious
refs.correction_note: stage1: §220 makes solitude+preoccupation the activating agent, not the opus; agency moved to the artifex with the conditions carried in the relation
refs.vocabulary_note: cross-vendor PARTIAL (b-cw13-4): text says 'the alchemist'; artifex is the standing node — synonym normalization, both-defensible

qualifiers.carrier: the adept, whose wholeness it is
qualifiers.condition: if the work is to reach its goal
qualifiers.modality: obligation (“must”), and a restoration rather than a novelty: “what she was from the beginning”
qualifiers.note: the return to the watery realm is the other half of the original predicate and is carried as a split; the text attaches the stated condition to that return.

refs.quote: Melusina, the deceptive Shakti, must return to the watery realm … must become what she was from the beginning: a part of his wholeness.

qualifiers.carrier: its strange and significant workings, which are the thing actually observed
qualifiers.note: the text's locus is “the manifestations of the unconscious,” and what is observed there are the workings of the lumen naturae rather than the lumen naturae itself; both are held in carrier and here. The identification with the natural spirit is a separate claim and is carried as a split.

refs.quote: The lumen naturae is the natural spirit, whose strange and significant workings we can observe in the manifestations of the unconscious

qualifiers.scope: the conscious attitude, which is what the text names rather than consciousness at large
qualifiers.modality: “for the most part functionally, though it sometimes corrects them by force”; given as what psychological research has come to realize
qualifiers.note: the text's object is “the biases and aberrations of the conscious attitude”; “aberrations” does not fit the predicate and is recorded here.

refs.quote: the unconscious is not just a “subconscious” appendage … is a largely autonomous psychic system for compensating the biases and aberrations of the conscious attitude

qualifiers.scope: in the Vita longa procedure Jung is reading (“here”), as the route to immortality
qualifiers.modality: “less by word than by deed,” and, Jung adds, without the least sign of any conflict with the orthodox Christian standpoint
qualifiers.note: the text says the sacraments of the Church; the object node is Christianity. The replacing term is the “sacrament” of the opus alchymicum in quotation marks.

refs.quote: the sacraments of the Church. These are here replaced by the “sacrament” of the opus alchymicum , less by word than by deed

qualifiers.scope: the mighty old oak of the fairytale, proverbially the king of the forest and so the most markedly personal of the contents of the unconscious
qualifiers.note: the text adds that it is “a symbol of the source and goal of the individuation process” and stands for the still unconscious core of the personality. The proverbial kingship is a ground for the claim, not a separate assertion about the world, so it is kept in scope.

refs.quote: The mighty old oak is proverbially the king of the forest. … It is the prototype of the self

qualifiers.scope: in psychological terms
qualifiers.modality: a conditional restatement of the fairytale's image: “this would mean that…”
qualifiers.note: the text presses the same claim further — “indeed in the body's chemical elements” — which is an intensification of this predicate rather than a second claim.

refs.quote: In psychological terms, this would mean that the self has its roots in the body, indeed in the body’s chemical elements.

qualifiers.scope: the pagan god Mercurius, whom the fairytale names as the spirit in the bottle and whom Jung couples with Wotan
qualifiers.modality: reported as the fairytale's interpretation of the evil spirit; the agent in the text is “the influence of Christianity”
qualifiers.note: the forced descent is the other conjunct, has its own object, and is carried as a split.

refs.quote: Our fairytale thus interprets the evil spirit as a pagan god, forced under the influence of Christianity to descend into the dark underworld

qualifiers.scope: in East and West alike, as alchemy's core
qualifiers.note: the text specifies the Gnostic doctrine of the Anthropos and adds that alchemy “by its very nature has the character of a peculiar doctrine of redemption.”

refs.quote: alchemy contains as its core the Gnostic doctrine of the Anthropos

qualifiers.scope: Mercurius as the revelatory light of nature
qualifiers.note: the text's word is “hell-fire”; ignis gehennalis is the graph's label. Jung qualifies the identity in the next clause: the hell-fire is “in some miraculous way… none other than a rearrangement of the heavenly, spiritual powers in the lower, chthonic world of matter.”

refs.quote: Mercurius, the revelatory light of nature, is also hell-fire
refs.vocabulary_note: cross-vendor PARTIAL (b-cw13-4): text says 'hell-fire'; ignis-gehennalis is the standing Latin node, wording acknowledged — both-defensible

qualifiers.scope: the “philosophic” Mercurius, so dear to the alchemist as the transformative substance
qualifiers.modality: “obviously”
qualifiers.note: the text adds the circumstance: such projection “always takes place when the inquiring mind lacks the necessary self-criticism in investigating an unknown quantity.”

refs.quote: the philosophic Mercurius, so dear to the alchemist as the transformative substance, is obviously a projection of the unconscious

qualifiers.scope: within the earth, in Penotus' formulation, which Jung quotes as stressing the corporeal aspect
qualifiers.modality: quoted from Penotus, a sixteenth-century pupil of Paracelsus, not asserted in Jung's own voice
qualifiers.note: Penotus' predicate is “nothing other than the spirit of the world become body within the earth”; “become body” is rendered as embodiment so that the frozen object can name the spiritus mundi.

refs.quote: nothing other than the spirit of the world become body within the earth
refs.source: Penotus (sixteenth century), a pupil of Paracelsus, quoted by Jung

qualifiers.note: the text's terms are “the Anthropos idea” and “the psychological concept of the self,” so the coincidence is between idea and concept; Jung offers the atman and purusha doctrines and alchemy as proof.

refs.quote: I would like to emphasize once again that the Anthropos idea coincides with the psychological concept of the self

qualifiers.carrier: his unity, which is at the same time a trinity and is what carries the reference
qualifiers.modality: “clear reference”, but expressly not derivation: Jung adds that his triadic nature “does not derive from Christian dogma but is of earlier date”
qualifiers.note: the object is the Holy Trinity.

refs.quote: The unity of Mercurius is at the same time a trinity, with clear reference to the Holy Trinity

qualifiers.scope: Mercurius as senex (Mercurius senex)
qualifiers.note: the paragraph piles up the supporting identifications: Saturn is the father and origin of Mercurius, quicksilver comes “from the heart of Saturn or is Saturn,” and in Khunrath Mercurius is the “salt of Saturn.”

qualifiers.modality: emphatic: “actually… the devil himself”; reported as the received astrological and Gnostic view, corroborated in the second reference by the prima materia being “saturnine”
qualifiers.note: the maleficus half of the original predicate is a separate claim and is carried as a split.

refs.quote: Saturn is not only a maleficus but actually the dwelling-place of the devil himself

qualifiers.scope: the dark Mercurius, in his dark form
qualifiers.modality: an interpretive instruction from Jung: “must once again be understood as representing”
qualifiers.note: the text's phrase is “the initial nigredo state,” in which the nigredo is that initial state; putting “initial state of” into the predicate would wrongly imply the nigredo has an initial state of its own, so “initial” is recorded here. Jung's gloss follows: “the lowest being a symbol of the highest and vice versa.”

qualifiers.condition: by carrying out the reverse movement - starting from below, ascending on high, and returning to earth with the powers of Above and Below united in himself
qualifiers.note: Jung's wording is 'a nature contrary to that of Christ', i.e. contrary to Christ's nature; the same is said of the Gnostic Redeemers, kept as a further claim

qualifiers.scope: as the highest goal of the work, as against the prima materia of its lowly beginning

qualifiers.scope: more than with goldmaking and chemical research, which were themselves of great concern to it
qualifiers.modality: hedged: the concern 'appears to have been'
qualifiers.note: the concern was the experience of the unconscious; Jung explicitly declines the word 'investigation' - 'one cannot very well say the "investigation"'

refs.quote: But a still greater, more impassioned concern appears to have been—one cannot very well say the “investigation”—but rather the experience of the unconscious.

qualifiers.scope: in the roots of the tree
qualifiers.condition: though imprisoned in the bottle
qualifiers.note: found there 'as its quintessence and living numen'; the subject in the text is 'the mercurial spirit'

refs.quote: the mercurial spirit, though imprisoned in the bottle, is yet found in the roots of the tree, as its quintessence and living numen

qualifiers.carrier: the wholeness of the personality, which the self epitomizes and which by definition includes the collective unconscious
qualifiers.modality: by definition
qualifiers.note: Jung states two linked propositions rather than this one directly; the inclusion follows through wholeness, which is why that term is carried rather than dropped. The context is his claim about 'the collective nature of the self'

refs.quote: since the self epitomizes the wholeness of the personality. By definition, wholeness includes the collective unconscious

qualifiers.modality: attributed: 'according to alchemy'; Jung reports the identity and calls it a shocking paradox he sees no choice but to accept
qualifiers.note: the text's 'Holy Spirit'; the identity is the stronger of two claims - the weaker, partaking, is kept separate

qualifiers.scope: in the physical world
qualifiers.modality: 'at most' - Jung is denying that the alchemists meant Christ by their lapis
qualifiers.note: Jung's wording is 'a counterpart or analogy'

refs.quote: The lapis is at most a counterpart or analogy of Christ in the physical world.

qualifiers.condition: except by incontestable and unprovable faith
qualifiers.note: said in the course of the claim that Mercurius as deus terrestris has something of the deus absconditus, an essential element of the psychological self

refs.quote: the self cannot be distinguished from a God-image (except by incontestable and unprovable faith)

qualifiers.scope: a tension of opposites such as had never occurred before in the whole history of Christianity beginning with the Creation
qualifiers.condition: as a result of what is taught about Christ - especially the crystal purity dogma has bestowed on his figure - not of Christ's own teaching
qualifiers.note: the Antichrist is specified 'as Satan or the fallen angel'

qualifiers.modality: 'according to all the psychological rules'

guided.gloss: The stone the alchemists sought is a projection of the self.
The prima materia they worked on is the unconscious under another name.
The work itself pictures the process, stage by stage.
The marriage that completes the work: what unites the opposites.
The uniting substance stands for the deepest layer of the psyche.
So the correspondence is structural: a substance read as a person.

guidedReverse.gloss: Begin where the alchemist began: with the raw material in the vessel.
Mercurius, the substance that reconciles what will not mix.
The same substance, read as a layer of the psyche.
Salt: its bitterness turns out to name a person.
The work, followed to its end, is a process of becoming whole.
And the stone at the end of it is the self.
